patient.name: Lorraine Campbell
patient.complaint: Burning pain over the left forehead for 3 days, now with blisters
background: Had chickenpox as a child in Kingston, Jamaica
Grandson Theo, 4, has had chickenpox this week
Daughter Jade, 30, is 10 weeks pregnant and unsure if she had chickenpox

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a painful, unilateral, dermatomal vesicular rash (shingles) or a child with crops of lesions at different stages (chickenpox); Hutchinson's sign, post-herpetic neuralgia and pregnancy are the classic twists.

points: 3 days of **burning pain** over her left forehead.
Today: a band of **blisters** on the left forehead and scalp.

steps.lead: Lorraine had chickenpox (the **primary** infection) as a child. Her rash now is the same virus **reactivating**: shingles.
Lorraine fits shingles perfectly: **older**, **immunosuppressed** by methotrexate, and has had varicella before.

points: Vesicles on a red base, **left side only**.
Follows the **ophthalmic division** of the trigeminal nerve (V1).
There are **vesicles on the tip of her nose**.

steps.lead: Pain and fever before the rash, then a **painful, dermatomal, vesicular, unilateral** eruption: textbook shingles in Lorraine's V1 dermatome.

steps.q: Lorraine has vesicles on the tip of her nose. What does this sign predict?
steps.r: This is **Hutchinson's sign**: the nasociliary nerve also supplies the eye, so the risk of **ocular complications** is three-fold higher.

steps.lead: Lorraine's nose-tip vesicles mean **nasociliary** involvement; she needs a same-day eye assessment for **ophthalmic zoster**.
Lorraine is 71, so **post-herpetic neuralgia** is a real risk; the eye and secondary infection are the other worries.

steps.r: Typical shingles is a **clinical diagnosis**. Testing is only needed when the picture is uncertain.

glossary.VZV: Varicella zoster virus, the herpesvirus that causes chickenpox and shingles.
glossary.varicella: Chickenpox, the primary infection with varicella zoster virus.
glossary.herpes zoster: Shingles, reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in a sensory nerve.
glossary.shingles: Painful, one-sided, dermatomal blistering rash from reactivated varicella zoster virus.
glossary.chickenpox: Itchy, feverish childhood illness with spots at different stages at once.
glossary.dermatome: The area of skin supplied by a single spinal or cranial sensory nerve.
glossary.dermatomal: Following the distribution of one dermatome.
glossary.vesicles: Small fluid-filled blisters under 5 mm across.
glossary.macules: Flat, coloured spots on the skin.
glossary.papules: Small raised solid spots on the skin.
glossary.prodrome: Early symptoms, such as fever or pain, before the main illness appears.
glossary.Hutchinson's sign: Shingles vesicles on the tip of the nose, warning of eye involvement.
glossary.nasociliary nerve: Branch of the ophthalmic nerve supplying the nose tip and the eye.
glossary.ophthalmic zoster: Shingles of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, which can damage the eye.
glossary.post-herpetic neuralgia: Nerve pain that persists in the dermatome after the shingles rash has healed.
glossary.congenital varicella syndrome: Fetal damage from first-trimester chickenpox: low birth weight, limb hypoplasia and skin scarring.
glossary.aciclovir: Antiviral that blocks herpesvirus DNA replication; used for chickenpox and shingles.
glossary.valaciclovir: A prodrug of aciclovir taken less often.
glossary.famciclovir: An alternative oral antiviral for shingles.
glossary.gabapentin: Anticonvulsant used for neuropathic pain such as post-herpetic neuralgia.
glossary.pregabalin: A gabapentin-like drug for neuropathic pain.
glossary.amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant used at low dose for neuropathic pain.
glossary.duloxetine: SNRI antidepressant also used for neuropathic pain.
glossary.calamine lotion: Soothing pink lotion used to ease chickenpox itch.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen; avoided in chickenpox.
glossary.necrotising fasciitis: Rapidly spreading deep soft-tissue infection; a rare complication of chickenpox.
glossary.IgG: Antibody that shows past infection or immunity.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction: a test that detects viral DNA.
glossary.dorsal root ganglia: Clusters of sensory nerve cell bodies beside the spinal cord where VZV lies latent.
glossary.latency: A dormant phase where the virus persists without causing disease.
glossary.cell-mediated immunity: T cell immunity; when it falls, VZV can reactivate.
glossary.methotrexate: Immunosuppressant used for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis.
glossary.trigeminal nerve: Cranial nerve V; its ophthalmic branch is the classic site of facial shingles.

technique.stem: A 76 year old man has a 4 day history of burning pain over the right side of his forehead, followed by a vesicular rash on the right forehead and scalp that stops at the midline. There are vesicles on the tip of his nose. His right eye is red and watery.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of a painful forehead rash in an older man.

clues: vesicles on the tip of his nose
steps.x: Older age, **pain before rash**, unilateral V1 vesicles, **Hutchinson's sign**, eye involved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Shingles of the ophthalmic division: **herpes zoster ophthalmicus**.

elim: Conjunctivitis does not cause a dermatomal vesicular rash.
HSV keratitis gives a dendritic ulcer, not a V1 dermatomal rash.
Impetigo gives honey-crusted lesions, not dermatomal vesicles.
Trigeminal neuralgia is brief shooting pain with no rash.

steps.x: **C. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus.** Nose tip vesicles = eye at risk.

technique.stem: A 69 year old woman has a 2 day history of a painful band of vesicles on a red base across the left side of her chest, in the T5 dermatome, which does not cross the midline. She had chickenpox as a child. She is otherwise well and not immunosuppressed.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: Which test, if any, for a typical rash?
A **classic** dermatomal shingles rash in a well patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Shingles is diagnosed **clinically**.

elim: Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary.
IgG shows past infection, which she already has; it does not diagnose shingles.
Culture is slow and outdated.
PCR is for uncertain or atypical cases only.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis.** Typical shingles needs no test.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man who had a kidney transplant 2 years ago and takes tacrolimus has a 1 day history of a widespread vesicular rash spreading beyond several dermatomes. He is drowsy. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily

steps.x: Management of shingles: decide how severe.
Immunosuppressed, **disseminated** and systemically unwell: severe shingles.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe shingles: **IV aciclovir**.

elim: Oral aciclovir is for uncomplicated shingles.
Famciclovir is an oral alternative for mild disease.
Delaying antiviral in disseminated zoster risks encephalitis and pneumonitis.
Topical aciclovir is not effective for shingles.

steps.x: **A. IV aciclovir.** Severe or disseminated = IV.

technique.stem: A 73 year old woman has a painful vesicular rash in a band around the left side of her waist that stops exactly at the midline front and back. She had chickenpox 65 years ago.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the distribution of the rash?
o: Blood-borne spread of a new virus
Lymphatic spread from a primary lesion
Reactivation in one dorsal root ganglion spreading down its sensory nerve
Spread along a single motor nerve

steps.x: A mechanism: why is the rash in one band on one side?
Previous chickenpox, a **dermatomal**, unilateral rash: reactivation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Latent VZV in **one dorsal root ganglion** reactivates and travels down that **sensory nerve**.

elim: Viraemia gives widespread rash, as in chickenpox.
Immune complexes cause vasculitis, not dermatomal vesicles.
Lymphatics do not follow dermatomes.
VZV lies in sensory, not motor, ganglia; the rash is sensory skin.

steps.x: **D. Reactivation in a dorsal root ganglion.** One ganglion, one nerve, one dermatome.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man has a 3 day history of burning pain on the right side of his chest, followed by a band of vesicles on a red base from his spine to his sternum. The rash does not cross the midline. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A painful, unilateral, dermatomal vesicular rash preceded by burning pain in an older adult is herpes zoster (shingles).

steps.x: Diagnosis of a painful vesicular chest rash.
Older adult, **pain first**, then a **dermatomal, unilateral** vesicular rash.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Shingles.**

elim: Pemphigoid gives tense bullae on the limbs, not a dermatomal band.
Contact dermatitis is itchy and follows the contact area.
Impetigo gives honey-crusted lesions, usually on the face.
HSV gives localised grouped vesicles, usually lips or genitals.

steps.x: **C. Herpes zoster.** Pain, then a dermatomal band.

practice.stem: A 4 year old boy has had a fever for 2 days, followed by an itchy rash that began on his scalp and spread to his face and trunk. On examination there are macules, papules, vesicles and crusted lesions at the same time. His temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 110 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A febrile prodrome then an itchy rash from scalp to trunk with lesions at all stages simultaneously is chickenpox (varicella).

steps.x: Diagnosis of a childhood rash.
Prodrome, scalp to trunk, itch, **all stages at once**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chickenpox.**

elim: HFMD gives vesicles on hands, feet and mouth.
Impetigo gives honey-crusted lesions, no prodrome.
Measles is a maculopapular rash from behind the ears, with coryza and conjunctivitis.
Scarlet fever is a sandpaper rash with a strawberry tongue.

steps.x: **E. Varicella.** All stages together.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has shingles affecting the left forehead and upper eyelid, which started 1 day ago. Vesicles are present on the tip of her nose. Her visual acuity is currently normal.
practice.q: Which complication is she at greatest risk of?
practice.e: Vesicles on the nose tip (Hutchinson's sign) indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and a three-fold increased risk of ocular complications.

steps.x: Which complication does the sign predict?
V1 shingles with **Hutchinson's sign**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Eye involvement** (ophthalmic zoster).

elim: Encephalitis is rare and not predicted by this sign.
Pneumonitis is a risk in adult chickenpox.
Ramsay Hunt is facial nerve zoster with ear vesicles.
Trigeminal neuralgia is not a zoster complication; PHN is.

steps.x: **B. Ocular involvement.** Nose tip predicts the eye.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man had shingles in the left T6 dermatome 4 months ago. The rash has healed but he still has burning, shooting pain in the same area, worse with light touch from his clothes. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 144/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Persistent neuropathic pain in the dermatome after the shingles rash has resolved is post-herpetic neuralgia, due to ongoing nerve damage and inflammation.

steps.x: Diagnosis of pain after shingles.

clues: shingles in the left T6 dermatome 4 months ago
steps.x: Pain in the **same dermatome** after the rash, with allodynia: neuropathic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Post-herpetic neuralgia.**

elim: Costochondritis is anterior chest wall tenderness, not dermatomal.
Recurrence would produce a new vesicular rash.
No trauma; fractures are point tender.
Disc prolapse is rare in the thoracic spine and has no shingles link.

steps.x: **B. Post-herpetic neuralgia.**

practice.stem: A newborn baby has a low birth weight, an underdeveloped left leg and zigzag scarring of the skin over the same leg. His mother, who had never had chickenpox, had an itchy vesicular rash at 11 weeks of pregnancy.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: First-trimester chickenpox in a non-immune mother can cause congenital varicella syndrome: low birth weight, limb hypoplasia and skin scarring.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a congenital syndrome.
Non-immune mother, **first-trimester** chickenpox, limb hypoplasia and scarring.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Congenital varicella syndrome.**

elim: CMV causes deafness, microcephaly and periventricular calcification.
Rubella causes cataracts, deafness and heart defects.
Toxoplasmosis causes hydrocephalus and diffuse calcification.
Fetal alcohol gives facial features and growth restriction, not limb scarring.

steps.x: **D. Congenital varicella syndrome.** Limb hypoplasia + skin scarring.

practice.stem: A 6 year old girl with chickenpox has been given ibuprofen for 3 days. She now has a rapidly spreading, red, swollen area on her thigh around a lesion, with pain much worse than the appearance suggests. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 150 bpm and BP 82/48 mmHg.

steps.x: **D. Necrotising fasciitis.** Why NSAIDs are avoided in chickenpox.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant develops an itchy vesicular rash on her face and trunk 12 hours ago, 2 weeks after her son had chickenpox. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: A non-immune pregnant woman with a chickenpox rash should start oral aciclovir within 24 hours of rash onset.

steps.x: Management of chickenpox in pregnancy.
Pregnant, non-immune, rash under **24 hours**, well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral aciclovir** within 24 hours.

elim: Supportive care alone is for children or immune women.
NSAIDs are avoided in chickenpox and in later pregnancy.
The live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy and does not treat infection.
Immunoglobulin is for exposure before a rash, not once it has appeared.

steps.x: **C. Oral aciclovir.** Non-immune, rash, within 24 h.

practice.stem: A 5 year old boy has a 2 day history of chickenpox. He is drinking well and playing. His mother asks how to manage his fever and itch. His temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. He has no medical problems.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Uncomplicated chickenpox in a child is managed supportively with calamine lotion and paracetamol; NSAIDs are avoided because of the risk of necrotising fasciitis.

steps.x: Management of uncomplicated chickenpox in a child.
Well, immunocompetent child: **supportive** care.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Calamine and paracetamol**, off school until crusted.

elim: NSAIDs raise the risk of necrotising fasciitis.
Aciclovir is not routine in healthy children.
No bacterial infection to treat.
Steroid cream does not help and may worsen infection.

steps.x: **A. Calamine lotion and paracetamol.**

practice.stem: A 74 year old man who takes prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica develops shingles in the left T8 dermatome. He had chickenpox as a child. He asks where the virus has been for the last 65 years.
practice.q: In which site has the virus most likely been latent?
practice.e: After primary infection, VZV establishes latency in the dorsal root ganglia and reactivates when cell-mediated immunity declines, as with age and steroids.

steps.x: Where does VZV hide?
Reactivation in a **sensory** dermatome, triggered by immunosuppression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dorsal root ganglia.**

elim: Anterior horn cells are motor; polio, not VZV, targets them.
B cells are the latency site for EBV.
Keratinocytes are infected during the rash but are not the latency site.
Schwann cells are not the reservoir.

steps.x: **C. Dorsal root ganglia.**
